title: How many Major Atlantic Hurricanes will occur in the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the number of major Atlantic hurricanes that occur between June 1, 2026, and November 30, 2026, inclusive, as reported by the [National Hurricane Center (NHC)](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/?atlc) of the United States National Weather Service on December 1, 2026.
fine_print: The question will be resolved using storm reports and data published by the National Hurricane Center as of December 1, 2026. Any subsequent revisions upgrading or downgrading a storm's intensity will not be considered. The NHC [Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2024/) and [Monthly Atlantic Tropical Weather Summary](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/text/MIATWSAT.shtml) may be used.
background:
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30, with peak activity occurring in August, September, and October. Major hurricanes, classified as Category 3 or higher on the [Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutsshws.php), have sustained wind speeds of at least 111 miles per hour (178 km/h) and can cause significant damage and loss of life.

As of August 2026, no major hurricanes have taken place during the 2026 season, with only 4 named storms and a total [accumulated cyclone energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy) of only 3.2.

On August 6, [NOAA released](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/hurricane.shtml) a forecast of a 70% probability for the following ranges:

* 7-13 Named Storms, including the 2 named storms that had been recorded to that point
* 2-6 Hurricanes
* 0-2 Major Hurricanes
* Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) range of 30-90% of the median, including the 3% that had been recorded to that point

If fewer than 2 Major Hurricanes occur, it would be the fewest since 2013.

comments.text:
The tropical storm is located in the southwestern Gulf just off the eastern coast of Mexico. Isaias has winds of 40 mph and it is expected to become a hurricane on Thursday, then rapidly strengthen to at least a Category 2 by Friday evening in the central Gulf. 

The storm's impacts will likely be along and east of its path. This storm is expected to benefit from water temperatures well into the 80s in the Gulf, plenty warm for intensification over the few days.

But with the jet stream sagging far to the south, Isaias will have to battle wind shear.

That matters because wind shear is hostile for developing and active tropical systems, tilting them or sometimes even outright preventing them from developing.

For now, the most likely intensity near landfall is a Category 2 hurricane.

Source:

[https://weather.com/2026/10/07/storms/hurricane/tropical-storm-hurricane-isaias-gulf-coast-louisiana-florida](https://weather.com/2026/10/07/storms/hurricane/tropical-storm-hurricane-isaias-gulf-coast-louisiana-florida)

comments.author: sai_39
comments.text:
[Tropical Depression Nine](https://prod-west-nhc.woc.noaa.gov/text/refresh/MIATCDAT4%2Bshtml/070255.shtml) has actually formed in the Gulf, and NHC now forecasts it to intensify rapidly and peak around 85 kt / 100 mph, which is a strong Category 2 hurricane. The Category 3 threshold is 96 kt / 111 mph, so the official forecast is only \~11 kt below the resolution threshold. 

NHC's latest forecast has roughly:

* Oct. 7: tropical storm
* Oct. 8: strengthening tropical storm → hurricane
* Oct. 9: **85 kt / 100 mph**
* Oct. 10: **85 kt / 100 mph**
* then rapid weakening after landfall.

NHC explicitly says the only limiting factor appears to be the southwesterly shear, which is forecast to strengthen as the cyclone approaches the northern Gulf Coast. Its intensity forecast follows the relatively aggressive Google DeepMind and HCCA guidance.

comments.author: sai_39
sai_39
comments.text:
As of October 1, NHC's season summary has 8 named storms, 0 hurricanes, 0 majors and 10.8 ACE. For context, the [normal 1991–2020](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/Background.html) Atlantic season produces approximately 14.4 named storms, 7.2 hurricanes, and 3.2 major hurricanes. So we're not dealing with an ordinary slightly-below-average season.

There seems to be no obvious imminent candidate. On September 30: 

* Hanna had become post-tropical.
* NHC showed **no Atlantic disturbances** in its current outlook.
* The prior September 29 Tropical Weather Outlook explicitly said tropical cyclone formation was not expected during the [following seven days](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/text/refresh/MIATWOAT%2Bshtml/310501_MIATWOAT.shtml).

As others pointed out the El Niño signal seems to be extremely hostile. [NOAA's](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/hurricane.shtml) seasonal hurricane analysis explicitly expected the developing strong/very strong El Niño to generate above-normal vertical wind shear over the Atlantic Main Development Region, potentially overwhelming locally favorable Atlantic SST conditions.  

Also, 2026 has been exceptionally active in the Pacific while the Atlantic has failed to produce even one hurricane. This is consistent with the expected ENSO pattern.  [AP News](https://apnews.com/article/pacific-hurricanes-el-nino-ec5961dffe9cf90d690811592ebd4c4e)

A [recent analysis](https://climateimpactcompany.com/climate-research-major-hurricanes-during-strong-el-nino-years-2-2/) identifies 1965, 1972, 1982, 1997 and 2015 as years with ONI (operational nino index) above +1.5 during Aug–Oct. Their full-season Atlantic major-hurricane counts were: 

* 1965: 1
* 1972: 0
* 1982: 1
* 1997: 1
* 2015: 2

The notable warning example is 2015 Joaquin. Joaquin was only a hurricane during September 30 and rapidly became a major right around the Sep 30/Oct 1 boundary, eventually reaching Category 4.

I am assigning \~17% at least one more storm because research using 1950–2019 data finds that October–November historically produces on average:

* 2.7 named storms
* 1.5 hurricanes
* 0.5 major hurricanes

About 20% of all Atlantic major-hurricane formations occur in October–November. [American Meteorological Society Journals](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/103/1/BAMS-D-20-0312.1.xml)

The main upside risk is [NOAA's late-September](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/ghaz/index.php) subseasonal discussion indicated that an evolving intraseasonal signal could temporarily weaken the intense El-Niño-related shear over Mexico, the Gulf and parts of the Caribbean, making tropical development somewhat more favorable. But there was substantial model uncertainty.
